messages.author: 936ef8c6d12fc338
messages.subject: ar1 vs rw1
parts:
Dear all,

I've fit two simple models, one with ar1 and one with rw1. Both have an overall intercept and and an iid random effect.

f(Hour, model = "ar1") + f(ID, model = "iid")
f(Hour, model = "rw1") + f(ID, model = "iid")

Both models have very similar fitted values with very similar credible intervals. What puzzles me is that the credible intervals for the Hour random effect and the credible interval for the global intercept are very different. These credible intervals for the ar1 model are about 5 times wider than those for the rw1 model. I would expect to see wide credible intervals for the fitted values when the individual terms have wide credible intervals.

Could someone explain what is going on?

Best regards,

ir. Thierry Onkelinx

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] ar1 vs rw1
parts:
For models with only weak identifiability (large intercept and short range ar1 is hard to distinguish from small intercept and long range ar1, for example) will have strong posterior negative correlations between the effect.
The marginal uncertainties can then be much higher than the uncertainty of their sum. This is quite common.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] ar1 vs rw1
parts:
If the data are well represented by a random walk, then yes, those two models should be very similar to that, with a large ar-coefficient.

Setting a sumtozero constrain for _all_ ar1 models is tempting, but is the wrong thing to do in many situations.
With only a single realisation, it comes down to prior information and domain specific knowledge; if the model is only used for interpolation/smoothing, then it doesn’t matter as much if the interpretation of each model component is different, but since imposing constraints fundamentally _changes_ the model (and this is also true of the rw1 model itself; there was a discussion about this a few months back, regarding intrinsic random field models, that I believe was on this list...) it’s not a universally appropriate approach.

The only “objective” way out is to have multiple realisations, where e.g. the intercept parameter is the same for each realisation, so that the model is properly identifiable.

Finn
